missions/african-initiated-churches/name: African-initiated churches and prophets (Harris, Kimbangu, Aladura, Shembe)
missions/african-initiated-churches/stat: Active and numerous, though increasingly overshadowed since the 1980s by newer Pentecostal-charismatic churches. Several (Kimbanguists, Church of the Lord Aladura, and others) joined the World Council of Churches, and the Organization of African Instituted Churches (1978) gives the movement a common voice; the Zion Christian Church and the Shembe churches remain among the largest religious bodies in southern Africa.
missions/african-initiated-churches/summ: From the 1880s onward Africans founded churches of their own, first by seceding from mission churches over racism and control (the ‘Ethiopian’ churches), then through prophets such as William Wade Harris, Garrick Braide, Simon Kimbangu, Isaiah Shembe, Engenas Lekganyane, Joseph Babalola and Josiah Oshitelu, who preached repentance, burned charms, healed by prayer and gathered hundreds of thousands into churches led entirely by Africans. These ‘African Initiated’ (or Independent, or Instituted) Churches translated Christianity into African idioms of healing, prophecy, dreams and communal ritual, and became the first large-scale proof that the faith could flourish beyond missionary control.
missions/african-initiated-churches/stor:
The first African-initiated churches were protests. In Lagos in 1888 members of the American Southern Baptist congregation left to form the Native Baptist Church; in 1891 Anglicans unhappy with missionary control formed the United Native African Church; and the humiliation of Bishop Samuel Ajayi Crowther, whose Niger Mission was dismantled by young CMS missionaries in 1890–91, became a lasting symbol of why Africans might need churches of their own. In South Africa the Wesleyan minister Mangena Mokone founded the Ethiopian Church in Pretoria in 1892, taking the name from Psalm 68:31 (‘Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God’). These ‘Ethiopian’ churches usually kept mission doctrine and liturgy but insisted on African leadership; the Swedish missionary-bishop Bengt Sundkler later distinguished them from the ‘Zionist’ type, which reshaped worship itself.

The second wave was prophetic. In 1910, imprisoned in Liberia, the Grebo teacher William Wade Harris experienced a vision of the Archangel Gabriel; in 1913–14 he walked barefoot along the coast of the French Ivory Coast into the British Gold Coast in a white gown, carrying a cross, a Bible and a calabash. In roughly eighteen months he baptised perhaps 100,000–120,000 people, ordered fetishes burned, preached the Sabbath and the Ten Commandments, tolerated polygamy and told converts to wait for teachers ‘with the Book’. The French deported him in 1914–15, but his converts built chapels and waited; when the Wesleyan missionary William Platt arrived in 1924 he found tens of thousands ready to become Methodists, while others formed the Harrist Church. In the Niger Delta, Garrick Braide’s healing revival (1915–16) produced the Christ Army Church after the Anglicans disowned him and the colonial government jailed him.

In the Belgian Congo, Simon Kimbangu, a Baptist catechist trained by the Baptist Missionary Society, began healing at Nkamba in April 1921. Crowds abandoned mission stations and plantations; the colonial state, fearing insurrection, arrested him within months. Sentenced to death, commuted to life, he spent thirty years in prison at Élisabethville (Lubumbashi), dying there in 1951. His followers, persecuted and deported for decades, emerged as the Église de Jésus-Christ sur la Terre par son envoyé spécial Simon Kimbangu, officially recognised on the eve of independence in 1959 and admitted to the World Council of Churches in 1969. In South Africa, Isaiah Shembe founded the amaNazaretha (Nazareth Baptist Church) in 1910 at Ekuphakameni near Durban, composing hymns, instituting a Saturday Sabbath and an annual pilgrimage to the mountain Nhlangakazi; Engenas Lekganyane, drawing on the Zionist movement that had come from John Alexander Dowie’s Zion City, Illinois, founded the Zion Christian Church around 1924, whose Easter gatherings at Moria now draw crowds counted in the hundreds of thousands to over a million.

In western Nigeria the influenza pandemic of 1918 gave rise to prayer groups (the ‘Precious Stone’ society at Ijebu-Ode) which rejected Western medicine and practised healing by prayer — hence the Yoruba name Aladura, ‘owners of prayer’. Moses Orimolade and the young visionary Christiana Abiodun Akinsowon founded the Cherubim and Seraphim in Lagos in 1925; Josiah Oshitelu founded the Church of the Lord (Aladura) at Ogere in 1930; and in the same year Joseph Ayo Babalola’s revival at Ilesha brought mass conversions and, after a failed partnership with the British Apostolic Church (broken partly over the use of medicine), the Christ Apostolic Church (1941). Samuel Oshoffa’s Celestial Church of Christ, founded at Porto-Novo in Dahomey in 1947, spread back into Nigeria and later to the diaspora in Europe and North America.

These churches agreed with the missions on much: the Bible (often in translation made by missionaries), the Trinity in most cases, the rejection of ancestral shrines and charms, baptism and the authority of Christ. They disagreed over who held authority, how the Spirit was experienced and what African custom could be kept. Many accepted polygamous converts, used drums and dance, white garments, holy water and sacred sites, and gave prophets, visions and healing a central role. Missionaries and many African Protestants long called them ‘syncretistic’ or ‘nativistic’; scholars such as Bengt Sundkler, Harold Turner, J. D. Y. Peel, Allan Anderson and Kwame Bediako later argued that most were authentic attempts to read the Bible through African questions about evil, misfortune and healing, while acknowledging that some movements did drift into messianism around the founder.

After independence the movement grew and diversified. In Zimbabwe the Johane Masowe and Johane Marange apostolic churches (from 1932) gathered huge followings; in Kenya the Akurinu and Legio Maria (1963) arose; in Zambia Alice Lenshina’s Lumpa Church ended in a tragic armed confrontation with the new state in 1964. Estimates of membership vary widely, but by the late twentieth century African Initiated Churches were commonly counted in the tens of millions across the continent. Since the 1980s, newer Pentecostal and charismatic churches have drawn many younger urban Africans away from the white-garment churches, often criticising them as mixed with traditional religion, while themselves adopting much that the AICs pioneered — healing, deliverance, prophecy and African leadership.
missions/african-initiated-churches/beli: The Bible, read directly and often literally in vernacular translation, as the authority above missionary tradition and denominational custom.

God’s power over witchcraft, evil spirits and misfortune, shown through healing by prayer, holy water and the laying on of hands rather than (in many Aladura and Zionist churches) through Western medicine.
The continuing gift of prophecy, visions and dreams, so that God speaks to African prophets as he did to Old Testament prophets.
Strong Old Testament emphases: the Sabbath in some churches, food and purity laws, sacred mountains and pilgrimage, and the founder as a Moses- or Elijah-like figure.
Rejection of ancestral shrines, charms and ‘fetishes’, often more radical than the mission churches, combined with acceptance of some customs (polygamy, drums, dance) that missions forbade.
In some movements, a high or messianic view of the founder (Shembe among the amaNazaretha, Kimbangu in later Kimbanguist teaching), which other Christians regard as a departure from orthodoxy.
missions/african-initiated-churches/stra: Itinerant prophets who walked from village to village calling for repentance, burning charms and baptising whole communities, as Harris did along the Ivory Coast in 1913–15.
Healing services and prayer camps that met urgent needs left unaddressed by mission medicine and colonial health services.
Indigenous hymnody, dance, drumming and white robes that made worship recognisably African and easy to transmit orally.
Holy cities and pilgrimage centres (Nkamba, Ekuphakameni, Moria, Ogere, Ilesha) that gave dispersed members a shared sacred geography.
Lay and charismatic leadership, including women prophets, without the long seminary training and missionary approval required by mission churches.
Migration networks that carried the churches to the mines and cities of southern Africa and later to London, Paris and North America.
missions/african-initiated-churches/grou: Coastal peoples of Côte d’Ivoire and western Ghana (Adjukru, Alladian, Ebrié, Nzima and others) through Harris’s preaching of 1913–15.
The Bakongo of the Lower Congo, among whom Kimbanguism became a mass movement despite decades of colonial repression.
Yoruba communities of western Nigeria and Benin through the Aladura churches.
Zulu-speaking peoples of Natal through Shembe’s amaNazaretha.
Northern Sotho, Pedi and migrant mine workers across South Africa, Zimbabwe and Botswana through the Zion Christian Church and other Zionist churches.
Shona-speaking Zimbabweans through the vaPostori (apostolic) churches of Johane Masowe and Johane Marange.
African migrants in Britain, France and the United States, among whom Cherubim and Seraphim, Celestial and Christ Apostolic congregations were founded from the 1960s.
missions/african-initiated-churches/chal: Colonial repression: Harris was deported, Braide jailed, Kimbangu imprisoned for thirty years and tens of thousands of his followers deported to distant parts of the Congo.
Hostility or condescension from mission churches, which often disciplined members who joined them and labelled them ‘sects’ or ‘syncretist’.
Limited theological education, which made it hard to train leaders and to answer charges of heterodoxy.
Succession disputes on the death of founders, which split the amaNazaretha, the Zion Christian Church and others into rival branches.
Competition since the 1980s from Pentecostal and charismatic churches that appeal to younger, urban and educated Africans.
The difficulty of applying healing teaching amid HIV/AIDS and other epidemics without discouraging medical treatment.
missions/african-initiated-churches/harm: Some churches forbade medicine and hospital treatment, with documented cases of preventable deaths, especially of children, in faith-healing communities.
Witch-finding and accusations made by some prophets stigmatised vulnerable people, particularly elderly women and children.
Founder-centred teaching sometimes turned into messianism and the cult of a ruling family, with church property and authority passed down hereditary lines.
Alice Lenshina’s Lumpa Church, withdrawing from the state, clashed with Zambian nationalists and troops in 1964; several hundred people died on all sides.
Acceptance of polygamy and of the prophet’s authority over marriage sometimes entrenched the subordination of women and child marriage in particular communities.
missions/african-initiated-churches/deve: Demonstrated, decades before decolonisation, that Africans could lead, finance and multiply churches without missionary control.
Created a large body of African Christian hymnody, liturgy and ritual, such as Shembe’s hymns, which is now studied as a major religious literature.
Anticipated and shaped African Pentecostalism’s emphasis on healing, deliverance and prophecy, and its engagement with the spirit world.
Provided mutual aid, moral discipline (abstinence from alcohol and tobacco) and community for migrants and the urban poor.
Prompted African theologians (Mbiti, Bediako, Oduyoye) and Western scholars to rethink ‘syncretism’ and to treat African culture as a vehicle for the gospel.
Gave Africa an early ecumenical voice through WCC membership (Kimbanguists 1969) and the Organization of African Instituted Churches (1978).
missions/african-initiated-churches/outc: African Initiated Churches proved that Christianity in Africa did not depend on missionaries, and they prepared the ground for the explosive growth of African Christianity after 1960. They remain a large and distinctive family, though many members have moved to newer Pentecostal churches.
missions/african-initiated-churches/keyP: Preached across the Ivory Coast and western Gold Coast in 1913–15, baptising perhaps 100,000 or more.
Deported by the French; his converts became Methodists, Catholics or members of the Harrist Church.
Healing ministry of 1921 that drew crowds from mission stations.
Imprisoned for thirty years; the Kimbanguist Church became one of Africa’s largest independent churches.
Prophet, hymn-writer and founder of the amaNazaretha
Founded the Nazareth Baptist Church in 1910 with Sabbath worship, pilgrimage and Zulu hymnody.
His church continues under rival branches led by his descendants.
Led the 1930 Ilesha revival of healing and mass conversion.
Revered as spiritual founder of the Christ Apostolic Church.

The movement fragmented into many branches but spread across Nigeria and the diaspora.

Healing, purity rules and the holy city of Moria.

Prophetic visions and a written ‘holy script’; founded his church in 1930.
The church spread to Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ghana and Britain and joined the WCC in 1975.
Healing and anti-charm revival in the Delta in 1915–16.

missions/african-initiated-churches/coun: Nigeria

Birthplace of the earliest secessions (Native Baptist Church 1888, United Native African Church 1891) and of the Aladura movement after 1918, including the Cherubim and Seraphim, the Church of the Lord and the Christ Apostolic Church.
South Africa
Home of the Ethiopian churches (Mokone, 1892) and of the Zionist family, including Shembe’s amaNazaretha (1910) and the Zion Christian Church (c. 1924).
Côte d’Ivoire
Scene of Harris’s mass baptisms of 1913–14 and seat of the Harrist Church.
Ghana
Harris preached around Axim and Apollonia in 1914; later many independent and spiritual churches arose, including the Musama Disco Christo Church (1922).
Liberia
Harris’s homeland, where his prophetic call came in prison in 1910.
Democratic Republic of the Congo
Kimbangu’s healing movement and the persecuted Kimbanguist Church, recognised in 1959 and now one of Africa’s largest independent churches.
Benin
Samuel Oshoffa founded the Celestial Church of Christ at Porto-Novo in 1947.
Zimbabwe
The vaPostori apostolic churches of Johane Masowe and Johane Marange, recognisable by white robes and open-air worship, grew from 1932.
Kenya
Akurinu (Arathi) prophets arose among the Kikuyu from the late 1920s, and Legio Maria broke from Catholicism among the Luo in 1963; Nairobi hosts the Organization of African Instituted Churches.
Zambia
Alice Lenshina’s Lumpa Church grew rapidly in the 1950s before its violent suppression in 1964.
United Kingdom
Aladura churches (Church of the Lord, Cherubim and Seraphim, Celestial Church) were established in London from the 1960s among West African migrants and students.
missions/african-initiated-churches/jour: Prophet Harris’s walk along the Ivory Coast and Gold Coast
William Wade Harris with women companions Helen Valentine and Mary Pioka

Wearing a white gown and carrying a cross, Bible and calabash, Harris walked eastward along the coast, baptising whole villages and ordering charms burned. After a few months in the Gold Coast he returned to the Ivory Coast, where the French authorities arrested and expelled him in late 1914 / early 1915.
Simon Kimbangu: from Nkamba to prison in Élisabethville

After six months of healing ministry, Kimbangu was arrested in September 1921, sentenced to death (commuted by the Belgian king to life imprisonment) and taken some 2,000 km across the colony to Élisabethville, where he died in prison in 1951. Nkamba later became the Kimbanguist holy city, ‘New Jerusalem’.

Shembe instituted an annual January pilgrimage to the holy mountain Nhlangakazi, which he had climbed in obedience to a vision; the pilgrimage, with hymn-singing and sacred dance, remains the movement’s central rite.
missions/african-initiated-churches/rela: AIC migrants founded churches in Europe and North America from the 1960s, an early form of ‘reverse mission’.
The Kimbanguist Church (1969) and the Church of the Lord (Aladura) (1975) joined the World Council of Churches, which also supported AIC theological education.
Babalola’s movement affiliated with the British Apostolic Church in the 1930s and Zionist churches grew from Dowie- and Pentecostal-linked missions, though both relationships ended in separation.
missions/african-initiated-churches/agre: Shared the conviction that Africans must have the Bible in their own languages; vernacular Scripture was the seedbed of nearly every prophet movement.
Agreed on healing, prophecy, spiritual warfare and the immediacy of the Holy Spirit, which is why many scholars treat AICs as part of the wider Pentecostal-type family.
Echoed Henry Venn’s ideal of self-governing, self-supporting and self-propagating churches, which the CMS itself had abandoned after Crowther.
missions/african-initiated-churches/disa: The dismantling of Bishop Crowther’s Niger Mission in 1890–91 and missionary racism drove Nigerian Anglicans into the first African churches.
BMS and other Protestant missions in the Congo distanced themselves from Kimbangu in 1921 and disciplined members who followed him; reconciliation came only much later.
Babalola’s followers broke with the British Apostolic Church (1939–41) partly because the missionaries accepted medicine and quinine, which the Nigerians held contrary to faith healing.
Evangelical faith missions often regarded the white-garment churches as syncretistic and refused fellowship over polygamy, holy water and founder-veneration.
missions/african-initiated-churches/devi: Later Kimbanguist teaching identified Simon Kimbangu with the Holy Spirit (the promised Paraclete) and treated his sons as divine figures, a departure from historic Trinitarian doctrine that strained relations with other Protestants and the WCC.
Some amaNazaretha hymns and teaching present Shembe as a messianic intermediary for black people, which critics regard as replacing Christ.
Bans on all medicine in some Aladura and Zionist churches went beyond the founders’ emphasis on prayer and caused avoidable suffering.
Succession by heredity and the accumulation of wealth by prophet families moved some churches away from their founders’ ascetic simplicity.
